Mitigating Citation Bias in Psychology & Neuroscience

Dr. Dani Bassett at the University of Pennsylvania has shared tangible ways we can mitigate citation bias in our field. This includes code to evaluate article references lists, a Google Chrome extension that predicts gender of authors, and a Citation Diversity Statement template.

Hi, I’m Allison! I’m a developmental psychologist and SNF Paideia-Provost Postdoctoral Fellow at the University of Pennsylvania.

My research lies at the intersection of psychology and technology.
Specifically, I study how social technologies, like digital media, social robots, and AI chatbots, shape children’s and adolescents’ development. My current work examines adolescents’ AI chatbot use, its links to self-regulation, and AI-literacy interventions that support adaptive use. Previously, as an Impact Fellow at Children and Screens, I translated research on social technologies into resources for families and policymakers.
My graduate work was funded by the National Science Foundation Graduate Research Fellowship. For info about applying to this fellowship, see resources.

title: Research
text:
Adolescents and AI Chatbots






I’m currently an SNF Paideia-Provost Postdoctoral Fellow at the University of Pennsylvania, where I study how children’s and adolescents’ interactions with emerging technologies influence their development and well-being. At Penn, I’m examining how individual differences shape teens’ use of artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots, and how AI-literacy-based interventions may encourage adaptive use.




I’m committed to translating research on digital media use into evidence-based resources for policymakers, educators, and families. I recently completed an Impact Fellowship at Children and Screens: Institute of Digital Media and Child Development, and I contribute to the International Research-driven Alliance for AI Serving Every Child (iRAISE) coalition to promote developmentally aligned AI innovation and governance.

title: Research
section: Smartphone and Social Media Use Across Development
text:
Smartphone and Social Media Use Across Development






My dissertation examined how smartphone and social media use relate to the development of self-regulatory control from childhood through adolescence, using behavioral and neuroimaging (fMRI) data. Results from node-wise fMRI and DTI analyses were presented at Flux: The Society for Developmental Cognitive Neuroscience in 2026.

title: Research
text:
Human-Computer Interaction






In collaboration with the Development and Experience Center at Franklin & Marshall College, we’ve investigated how children learn from social robots (see our article in Scientific Reports and a news story about the collaboration here). We’ve also examined how children perceive text and images generated by artificial intelligence. This work received the 2025 Award for Excellence in Science at the Digital Media and Developing Minds International Scientific Congress and is now published in Technology in Society.

title: Research
text:
Stakeholder Research






Developers have proposed incorporating social technologies into classrooms to provide adaptive learning tools for students. We worked with teachers in the School District of Philadelphia to understand their thoughts, fears, and impressions of using such tools in their classrooms. I presented the results from this study at the American Educational Research Association Annual Meeting in 2024. See the slides here.

title: Research
text:
Quantitative Methods






Using data from the Baby’s First Years Project, I used different quantitative methods to investigate stress among mothers enrolled in the study. I presented a hierarchical linear model at the Society for the Study of Human Development conference in 2023, and a subsequent structural equation model on RPubs in 2024.

title: Research
section: Technology as a Scalable Diagnostic Tool
text:
Technology as a Scalable Diagnostic Tool






This work examines how technology, such as motion tracking tools, can be used to aid in diagnosis and support for autistic individuals. Specifically, I’ve worked to design a dance video game to engage adolescents in practicing motor skills at the Center for Autism Research at the Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia (CHOP), served as an avatar for the Computerized Assessment of Motor Imitation (CAMI) (study here, and news article here) at the Kennedy Krieger Institute, and contributed to work investigating how we can quantify social behaviors during child-clinician interactions with motion capture.
